title: Infra GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts & Networking, IaC Modules, CI/CD — Ops Playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary

This playbook consolidates operational guidance for: GPU fleet capacity management, cloud account and network topology standards, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and day-2 runbooks used by Infra and Platform teams. It is intended for on-call engineers, infra owners, and SREs responsible for provisioning, scaling, and operating Redwood’s inference capacity.

Goals

- Provide repeatable procedures for common events (capacity surge, region failover, module updates).
- Define IaC module ownership and release patterns to enable safe changes across the fleet.
- Standardize cloud account and VPC designs for predictable network security and peering.
- Document CI/CD patterns for module releases, AMI builds, and cluster rollouts.
- Capture alert thresholds, SLOs, and runbook steps for first responders.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: Infra Engineering (infra-gpu-capacity@redwood.com)
- Secondary owner: Platform (platform-ops@redwood.com)
- Pager rotation: eng-sre oncall via PagerDuty (team: ENG-SRE)
- Module owners: see Terraform modules table below

High-level Architecture (summary)

Redwood runs GPU-backed inference clusters across multiple cloud accounts and regions. Key components:

- GPU node pools (k8s/GKE + node pools or kOps clusters on AWS depending on account).
- Serving runtime services (inference-runtime, routing-proxy, model-cache) running in each cluster.
- Control plane (control-plane) in a dedicated management account with CI/CD and terraform state.
- Network topology: hub-and-spoke VPC model with transit gateway/filo peering for east-west model replication.

Standards and SLOs

- Cluster availability SLO: 99.9% per region for inference-runtime (monthly).
- Pod latency SLO: 95th percentile tail < 150ms for short requests (<= 256 tokens) under normal load.
- Capacity headroom target: maintain at least 20% spare GPU capacity for burst traffic per pool.
- Build pipeline SLO: module plan/apply jobs must complete or fail within 30 minutes for small modules; 2 hours for full cluster operations.

Capacity Planning and Sizing

1) Key inputs:
   - Peak concurrent tokens/sec per region (measure from api-usage dashboards).
   - Average tokens per request and model tokenization factor.
   - Model per-token GPU seconds (measured from benchmarking suite).

2) Simple capacity formula:
   - Required GPUs = ceil((peak_tokens_per_sec * avg_token_gpu_seconds) / tokens_per_gpu_sec)
   - Add 20% headroom and reserve N spare nodes for gradational failures (N = 2 min).

3) Example:
   - Peak tokens/sec = 1200
   - avg_token_gpu_seconds = 0.0005 (0.5ms per token)
   - tokens_per_gpu_sec = 2000 (measured for A100 80GB with optimized kernels)
   - Required GPUs = ceil((1200 * 0.0005) / (1/2000)) = ceil(600 / 2000) = 1 -> add headroom -> 2 GPUs pool (but actually use node sizing to match GPU counts per node).

Terraform / IaC Modules (catalog & patterns)

We maintain a small set of core modules stored in git under infra/terraform/modules. Module naming convention: module-<domain>-<resource>. Ownership, changelog, and semver tags are required for each module. Key modules:

| Module name | Purpose | Owner | Release repo | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| module-gke-cluster | Provision GKE clusters and node pools | infra-gke-team | git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/modules.git//module-gke-cluster | Supports node-pool gpu_type var |
| module-gpu-node | Node pool with GPU instance families, autoscaling groups | infra-gpu-team | git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/modules.git//module-gpu-node | Exposes gpu_count, machine_type, taints |
| module-vpc-hub | Hub VPC, TGW / peering and routing tables | infra-network | git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/modules.git//module-vpc-hub | Must be deployed before spokes |
| module-vpc-spoke | Tenant VPC with service endpoints and shared services | infra-network | git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/modules.git//module-vpc-spoke | Contains bastion and subnet mapping |
| module-iam-bases | Base IAM roles & service accounts | security | git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/modules.git//module-iam-bases | Follow least-privilege patterns |

Module release workflow (required)

1. Create feature branch in modules repo.
2. Bump module version in versions.tf / CHANGELOG.md.
3. Run terratest/unit tests locally (make test-module MODULE=module-foo).
4. Open PR with changelog and reviewer tag (owner listed in module metadata).
5. CI will run plan in a sandbox account (infra-sandbox) and post plan to PR.
6. After approval, maintainer merges and CI tags a semver release.
7. Consumers must update module references and run their repo-level plan/apply.

State management and isolation

- Each environment (sandbox, staging, prod) uses a separate Terraform workspace and remote state bucket (encrypted, versioned).
- State bucket naming: tfstate-<env>-<account-id>. Example: tfstate-prod-1234567890.
- Locking: DynamoDB state lock table or cloud-specific lock. Lock TTL: 1 hour.

CI/CD and Build Patterns

General patterns:
- All IaC modules and infra repos use the same pipeline template (gitlab-ci / GitHub Actions).
- Pipelines produce a plan artifact and a deterministic plan ID for approval.
- Sensitive applies for prod require manual approval from infra owners and a successful preflight test in staging.

Pipeline steps (modules):
1. lint (tflint, terraform fmt check)
2. unit tests (terratest)
3. plan in sandbox (use minimal changes)
4. publish plan artifact
5. optional manual approval (required for prod changes)
6. apply in target workspace (automated for non-prod; manual for prod)

Immutable AMI/Container builds for GPU nodes

- GPU AMIs are baked using Packer in infra/images repo. Packer build triggers on canary branch.
- Build pipeline tags images as redwood-gpu-ami:<kernel>-<cuda>-<sha>. Example: redwood-gpu-ami:ubuntu22.04-cuda12-3f7a2d9
- Node pools reference image_id variable; updates are rolled via cluster rolling update job that respects maxUnavailable 10%.

Network and Cloud Account Standards

Account separation
- Management (control-plane) account: CI/CD, secrets manager, terraform remote state.
- Prod account(s): inference clusters per region (prod-us-west-2, prod-eu-west-1).
- Shared services account: logging, observability, model-artifact storage.

VPC topology
- Hub VPC: centralized peering/transit gateway, NAT gateways, shared EFS/FSx where required.
- Spoke VPCs: per-cluster / per-tenant VPCs with private subnets and dedicated route tables.
- CIDR allocation: 10.<account-block>.<region-block>.0/20 per VPC. Reserve 10% for future expansion.

Peering & service connectivity
- Use TGW when supporting >5 spokes; otherwise use VPC peering and route propagation.
- ENCRYPTION: all transit traffic must use cloud provider encryption-in-transit features where supported.
- Required endpoints: S3/GCS, STS, KMS, ECR/GCR. Configure prefix lists for known service ranges.

Security controls and egress
- Egress proxy: all clusters egress through shared egress NAT and proxy (egress-proxy.redwood.svc).
- Bastion hosts: deployed in spoke public subnets with strict SSH guards and session recording.
- KMS keys: customer-managed keys for private deployments and prod artifact buckets.

Runbooks and Playbooks (day-2 operations)

1) Capacity Surge (high-level)
- Trigger: alerts when available GPU capacity < 20% in a region OR queuing > 30s for > 5 minutes.
- Primary actions:
  1. Check cluster autoscaler logs and metrics (kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler).
  2. Verify cloud quota (compute/GPU quotas) in cloud console with account owner.
  3. If autoscaler is healthy but capacity insufficient, scale node pool manually: terraform apply module-gpu-node with increased desired_count or create a new node pool with larger instance types.
  4. If quotas exhausted, open quota request with cloud provider and enable temporary cross-region fallback routing (see "Region fallback" section).
  5. Notify product owners and enable traffic shed policy (routing-proxy knob: percent_shed) if necessary.

2) Node/Instance failure causing degraded capacity
- Steps:
  1. Identify failing node: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady.
  2. Inspect instance status in cloud console and collect instance console logs.
  3. If instance is unrecoverable, cordon and drain node; the autoscaler should provision replacements. If not, trigger resize or fallback pool.
  4. Replace AMI if failure is image-related and start an image-gated rolling update.

3) CI/CD Plan Failure (infra module plan fails)
- Steps:
  1. Review plan artifact in CI job. Identify drift and missing variables or permissions.
  2. Run terraform plan locally with TF_LOG=DEBUG if needed.
  3. If failure due to state corruption, do not attempt ad-hoc state edits. Escalate to infra owner and create a dedicated incident.

4) Terraform state locker stuck
- Cause: stale lock in DynamoDB / backend.
- Steps:
  1. Confirm lock via aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-locks --key '{"LockID": {"S": "<workspace>"}}'
  2. Identify locking user from item metadata and contact them. If unavailable, use (infra-admin) to force-unlock via terraform force-unlock <ID>.
  3. Document the reason and rotate credentials if lock was malicious.

Rolling update and rollback guidance

- Canary first: deploy module changes to sandbox -> staging -> prod. Use blue/green or canary node pool updates for node image changes.
- Rolling update constraints: maxUnavailable 10%, maxSurge 2 nodes. For large clusters, perform staged updates by AZ.
- Rollback: revert module version in consumer repo and reapply. For stateful regressions, follow the incident-runbook and engage data services.

Observability and Alerts

Key dashboards:
- infra/gpu-capacity-overview: shows GPUs total/allocated/available, average utilization, 95th token latency.
- infra/autoscaler-health: cluster-autoscaler events, scale-up/scale-down counts, pending pods.
- infra/networking: TGW latency, route table anomalies, VPC flow logs errors.

Important alerts (examples):
- GPU_AVAILABLE_PERCENT < 20% sustained for 5m -> P1 page oncall.
- ClusterAutoscalerFailedScaleUp -> P1.
- TerraformApplyFailed (prod) -> P1 to owners.

Tooling and useful commands

- Check GPU pool status: kubectl -n inference get nodes -l nodepool=gpu -o wide
- Check queue/latency: curl -s https://observability-api.internal/metrics?query=service_latency | jq .
- Run module plan locally: TF_VAR_env=staging terraform plan -var-file=vars/staging.tfvars
- Force-unlock state: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>

Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- Direct edits in prod state: never manually mutate state unless a documented emergency process is followed.
- Large monolithic modules: keep modules small and composable. If a change affects multiple resources, break it into multi-step releases.
- Skipping staging: always validate node pool and AMI changes in a staging cluster that mirrors production AZ distribution.

Appendix: Quick reference snippets

1) Example module usage (consumer repo)

module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/modules.git//module-gpu-node?ref=v1.3.0"
  name = "prod-us-west2-gpu"
  gpu_count = 8
  machine_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  desired_count = 12
}

2) Autoscaler manual scale (k8s)

kubectl -n kube-system scale deployment cluster-autoscaler --replicas=3

3) Example CI check (GitHub Actions job snippet)

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=tfstate-${{ github.ref_name }}\"
